summary: Tests, round 1. Ten mutations RUN in a throwaway worktree (git worktree + staged patch), each verified to COMPILE (0 'error:' lines) and to have executed 212 tests over 29 XML files before any survival was claimed. KILLED, all by OneStreamPerConsumerTest: (1) dropping the grouping so each run gets its own Target again -- kills BOTH new tests; (2) open() handed only the first push -- kills aConsumerHoldingMANYRuns on the K-distinct-keys assertion; (3) the recorded push list truncated to its first element -- kills aSTREAMThatBROKE; (4) every push built from t.runs().get(0) -- killed on the distinct-key count; (5) K sinks opened but bytes written only to the first -- killed on `opens == 1` ('expected 1 but was 64'), which answers the question directly: aConsumerHoldingMANYRunsOfOneSegmentIsHandedTheBytesONCE cannot pass by opening K sinks and writing to one, and `bytes` really is the total length pushed to that consumer because the AtomicLong is shared by every sink the one Subscriber instance returns. So the headline contract of this task is genuinely pinned. SURVIVED: ByIdentity.equals switched to .equals (F1); complete() handed another consumer's push list (F2); the new for-loop in assembling() reduced to pushes.get(0) (F3); the modeFor fan-out argument switched from targets.size() to committed.runs().size() (F4); LinkedHashMap swapped for a plain HashMap (F5). ByIdentity.hashCode returning a constant also survives and is NOT reported: it stays consistent with equals, so it is an equivalent mutant on behaviour and costs only hash distribution -- no test could kill it. THE TWO ADAPTED FILES WERE NOT WEAKENED. Every `push -> ...` site became `pushes -> pushes.forEach(...)`, so each per-run observation is still recorded once per run, not once per consumer: AssembledServingPathTest:92, :140, :303, :310 (both minesLabels/theirsLabels and minesModes/theirsModes stay inside the forEach), :483, and AssembledServingPathFailureTest:119, :237, :459. aSegmentOfMANYRunsIsReadONCENotOncePerRun keeps `mine.addAll(...)` under an unchanged `singleElement()` plus the key/recordCount/firstOffset/segmentKey assertions, and its 8 subscribers are 8 DISTINCT lambda instances each holding one run, so grouping makes each Target size 1 and no observation is lost. No assertion in either file was loosened; the gets()==1, hasSize(64), containsOnly(PROXY) and containsExactlyInAnyOrder assertions are byte-identical to HEAD. aSTREAMThatBROKE's FALSIFIABILITY CLAIM IS HALF TRUE AND I TESTED BOTH HALVES. The second half is HONEST and verified: I replaced the once-only throw with an unconditional throw and re-ran against the no-grouping mutation -- aSTREAMThatBROKE then PASSES (only the other test fails), so a sink throwing on every write really would pin nothing. The first half is FALSE and is F6: HELD is 17 bytes and the policy is FetchPolicyConfig(MAX,MAX,1), so modeFor returns INLINE and writeHeldBytes makes exactly ONE write call per sink -- the sink throws on its only write having delivered ZERO bytes, not a prefix, and nothing 'part way through' happens. The `writes.getAndIncrement() == 0` guard discriminates across the four SINKS the old contract would have opened (they share the counter), not across writes within one stream. Tree untouched: all work done in a detached worktree under the scratchpad; `git diff --cached | sha256sum` re-checked immediately before recording and still 820e05fe.

findings.title: A consumer can be completed with ANOTHER consumer's push list and nothing fails
findings.failure_scenario: SURVIVING MUTATION, RUN not reasoned: `live.get(i).subscriber().complete(pushes.get(i), sink.delegate)` -> `complete(pushes.get(0), ...)`. Compiles, 212 tests run, all green. The new contract's whole subject is that a consumer is handed K pushes that are ITS OWN runs, and the `open` half of that is pinned (open() truncated to the first push is killed by aConsumerHoldingMANYRuns' distinct-key assertion) while the `complete` half is not pinned at all. Concrete bug this permits: consumer A subscribes runs {0,1} and consumer B subscribes runs {2,3} of one segment; B's complete() is invoked with A's pushes, so B is told it received partitions 0 and 1 at A's offsets and record counts, decodes A's stream identities over its own bytes, and advances the wrong offsets. It survives because the only two consumers in OneStreamPerConsumerTest hold the SAME four runs (so pushes.get(0) and pushes.get(1) are equal-valued) and because every other complete() in the suite discards its pushes argument. Closing it costs one case: two subscribers on DISJOINT run sets, assert each complete() receives exactly its own RunKeys. That is the complete-side twin of the comment AssembledServingPathTest:211-219 already writes for open().

findings.title: The new K-push loop in assembling() is unconstrained -- reduce it to the first push and the suite stays green
findings.failure_scenario: SURVIVING MUTATION, RUN: replace the new `for (Push push : pushes) { onSegment.accept(...); }` with a single `onSegment.accept` built from `pushes.get(0)`. Compiles, 212 tests, green. This loop is production code ADDED BY THIS DIFF and it is the only place the K pushes are fanned back out to a Consumer<Push>-shaped consumer, so under the mutation a node holding K runs of a segment is notified about run 0 and the other K-1 runs are silently never delivered -- the same record-loss shape the batched-delta test at AssembledServingPathTest:280-288 documents as 'silently, with the commit already durable'. It survives because every caller of assembling() (DefaultIngestTest:69, :151, :228, BulkThroughTheRealStackTest:98) subscribes exactly one RunKey per Subscriber instance, so K is always 1 and the loop body runs once whatever it contains. One case with a single assembling() subscriber on two RunKeys of one segment, asserting two accepted pushes with two distinct keys, closes it.

findings.title: ByIdentity's `==`-not-`equals` guard, which the javadoc spends a paragraph on, has no test
findings.failure_scenario: SURVIVING MUTATION, RUN: `o.subscriber == this.subscriber` -> `o.subscriber.equals(this.subscriber)`. Compiles, 212 tests, green. The javadoc at :330-334 states the hazard precisely -- 'two subscribers that merely compare equal are still two consumers, and merging them would hand one of them the other's stream' -- and nothing in the suite can tell the two implementations apart, because every Subscriber in the tree is a lambda or an anonymous class and so inherits identity equality. Concrete bug this permits: a consumer written as `record NodeSubscriber(String nodeId, Channel ch) implements Subscriber`, which is an entirely natural shape, has two live subscriptions on one node collapse into ONE Target -- one subscription's sink is never opened, never written and never completed, and its runs are lost with the commit durable and no error anywhere. The test is cheap: a value-equal Subscriber record, two instances that compare equal, subscribed to two RunKeys of one segment, assert TWO opens. Without it the whole ByIdentity type is executed but unconstrained.

findings.title: The fan-out argument to modeFor changed meaning in this diff and no test can see it
findings.failure_scenario: SURVIVING MUTATION, RUN: `new SegmentDelivery(heldBytes.length, true, targets.size(), false)` -> `... committed.runs().size(), false)`. Compiles, 212 tests, green. The comment added at :377-383 claims this number MOVED with M5.40a ('a handful of nodes holding many runs each looked like a large fan-out and could tip modeFor into a different mode than the traffic warranted') -- that is a claimed behaviour change with no falsifying test, which is the shape rule 4 exists to catch. It survives because no existing test both holds K>1 runs on one consumer and sits near a policy boundary: every fan-out assertion in the suite uses one run per subscriber, where the two expressions are equal. Minor rather than major only because the divergence is unreachable today -- FetchPolicy.wantsDirect needs capabilities.presignedUrls() and neither shipping backend reports it. It escalates the day a presigning backend lands: an inflated fan-out count flips modeFor's DIRECT arm, and publishSegment's DIRECT case throws IllegalStateException, so a wrong count there is a thrown delivery rather than a suboptimal one. One case asserting the mode chosen for one consumer x K runs against a threshold between 1 and K pins it.

findings.title: The LinkedHashMap comment asserts a test dependency that does not exist
findings.failure_scenario: SURVIVING MUTATION, RUN: `new LinkedHashMap<>()` -> `new java.util.HashMap<>()`. Compiles, 212 tests, green -- and deterministically so, not luckily: every ordering assertion the comment could mean is order-insensitive (AssembledServingPathFailureTest:140, :263, :490 all use containsExactlyInAnyOrder, and the by-index pairing inside deliver() is between its own parallel opened/pushes/live lists, which stay consistent under any map order). So the claim 'Tests that pair a subscriber with its sink by index depend on it' is false as written. This is prose at the weakest rung making an unfalsifiable promise about determinism: with identityHashCode keys a plain HashMap's order varies per JVM run, so if a future test ever DOES depend on delivery order it will be flaky rather than failing, and this comment will be read as the reason it cannot be. Either cut the sentence to the reproducibility argument alone, or add the assertion that makes it true.

findings.title: 'part way through' never happens: the sink throws on its only write, having delivered zero bytes
findings.failure_scenario: NOT a surviving mutation -- a MEASURED false statement in a test that is otherwise falsifiable, so minor. HELD is 17 bytes (line 43) and publishHeld uses FetchPolicyConfig(Long.MAX_VALUE, Long.MAX_VALUE, 1), so FetchPolicy.modeFor takes its first arm and returns INLINE, and the INLINE source is writeHeldBytes, which issues exactly ONE `sink.write(heldBytes, 0, heldBytes.length)` per sink. The fake therefore throws on its FIRST AND ONLY write and the consumer holds ZERO bytes, not the PREFIX the name and the javadoc at :96-104 describe; the real prefix case (sink accepts chunk 1, throws on chunk 2, Tracking marks it, complete is skipped) is covered at AssembledServingPathFailureTest:490-491, not here, and never with K>1 runs. What the `writes.getAndIncrement() == 0` guard actually discriminates is the four SINKS the old contract would have opened, which share the counter -- and that half of the javadoc's claim is TRUE and I verified it: replacing the guard with an unconditional throw and re-running against the no-grouping mutation leaves aSTREAMThatBROKE PASSING (only the sibling test fails), so an always-throwing fake really would pin nothing. Fix is either the name and the paragraph, or a policy that chunks the 17 bytes so the described scenario is the one executed.
